title: Corns and calluses: reducing pressure safely
intro: A corn is a small area of thickened skin, often with a dense centre that hurts when pressed. A callus is usually a broader patch of hard skin. Both commonly develop where skin repeatedly rubs or bears pressure. Removing the hard skin alone often gives only temporary relief unless the pressure causing it also changes.

sections.heading: Check what the painful patch actually is
paragraphs: Corns often occur over toe joints, between toes or on the sole. Those between toes can look softer because the area is moist. Tight shoes, rubbing seams, foot shape and altered walking patterns can concentrate pressure. Calluses can also form on hands using tools or instruments. A wart, splinter or other skin problem may look similar; do not dig into a lesion to find a supposed root. Corns are a response to pressure, not a contagious infection. If appearance is unusual, the diagnosis is uncertain or a patch bleeds, get it examined.

sections.heading: Some feet need professional care from the outset
paragraphs: If you have diabetes, poor circulation, reduced sensation, weakened immunity or fragile older skin, ask a clinician or foot specialist before attempting treatment. Lack of pain does not prove the skin underneath is safe when nerves are damaged. Do not cut, shave or chemically burn away the area. Check feet regularly, including the soles and between toes; use a mirror or trusted helper if needed. A new break in the skin, discharge, warmth, swelling or colour change deserves prompt advice, particularly with diabetes. Fever, spreading redness, a blackened area or a suddenly cold painful foot needs urgent assessment.

sections.heading: Relieve pressure in everyday situations
paragraphs: Choose supportive shoes with enough width and toe space, a low heel and a soft sole; check that socks and seams do not create new rubbing. Soft cushioning, an insole or a toe separator may help if correctly fitted. A pharmacist or podiatrist can distinguish a plain protective pad from a medicated remover and check placement. A badly positioned pad or cramped shoe can create extra pressure. Temporarily reduce long periods standing or walking if painful while arranging a practical alternative. Work footwear may need professional fitting or a different model that still meets workplace protection requirements.

sections.heading: Self-care is for intact skin without risk factors
paragraphs: For otherwise healthy feet, a brief warm-water soak may soften hard skin before very gentle use of a pumice stone or foot file. Stop before soreness or skin injury; never use blades, scissors or sharp corn cutters. Moisturiser can help dry skin, but avoid leaving moisture trapped between toes. Ask a pharmacist before using salicylic-acid corn treatments: these can damage surrounding skin and are unsuitable for some people. Do not apply them to broken or infected skin. The aim is gradual comfort, not removing all protective skin in one session. People with high-risk feet should follow their individual foot-care plan instead.

sections.heading: When a foot specialist can help
paragraphs: Arrange assessment for severe pain, difficulty doing normal activities, recurrent lesions or no improvement after roughly three weeks of suitable low-risk self-care. Seek help earlier for concerning changes. A podiatrist can confirm the diagnosis, safely reduce thickened skin and assess footwear, pressure distribution and toe deformity. Individual padding or insoles may reduce recurrence. Surgery is rarely needed and addresses a selected underlying structural problem rather than being the routine answer to a corn. Antibiotics are only relevant if infection is diagnosed; they do not remove pressure-related hard skin. Continued pressure means the corn may return even after successful removal.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: changing the source of rubbing
examples.text: A warehouse worker repeatedly trims a painful patch over a toe. A foot specialist finds that the safety boot presses on a bent toe. They arrange an adequately protective wider model and suitable cushioning, rather than relying on repeated removal alone.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: painless does not mean harmless
examples.text: A woman with diabetes notices a hard patch with a small dark spot underneath. Because sensation in her feet is reduced, she seeks prompt foot-care advice instead of using an acid plaster simply because the area does not hurt.
